Software engineers who fear that AI coding assistants are automating away the craft have it backward, according to Angie Jones, a prominent AI systems engineer and longtime advocate for testing and quality. Jones spent a Friday night building agents for operational tasks and realized the old "dev flow" thrill was intact — not despite the shift to AI but because of it. The widespread dread that coding assistants are stealing "the fun parts" of software engineering, she argues, is a failure of perspective. Engineering discipline has not been displaced; it has migrated up one layer of abstraction. Designing agentic systems exercises the same muscles — systems thinking, decomposition, workflow design, state management, security engineering — as traditional software, just with different primitives.
Jones grounds the argument in a concrete artifact she built: Relocation Scout, a persistent house-hunting agent. Rather than a one-shot prompt that ranks listings and stops, Relocation Scout is a reusable system with structured memory (implemented via Compendium Wiki), deterministic helper scripts for exact calculations, sub-agents for research tasks, skills that span markets, and human-in-the-loop guardrails for high-stakes actions. Its architecture serves as a live demonstration that building agents is software engineering, and that engineers should let agents handle code-writing grunt work while they reclaim the higher-order design challenge.
## Systems thinking and workflow design
The first engineering skill Jones exercises is **systems thinking**. An agent is not the system, she emphasizes; it is part of a system that includes files, tools, humans, and other agents. Before writing a single prompt, she considers the whole environment: what is this agent's job? What does it depend on? What happens when it breaks? "I want to treat it like any other component where it has boundaries and responsibilities, has dependencies, and ways that it can fail," she says. "That whole thought process, that's engineering."
Relocation Scout does not sit in isolation. It pulls in listings and neighborhood signals, weighs them against the user's criteria, and hands back a ranked shortlist. "What's this agent's job? What does it depend on? What happens if it breaks?" are the questions Jones asks before her coding agent touches a file.
**Workflow design** follows directly. A goal — "review this listing" — is insufficient; an agent needs a path. Jones defines every workflow as containing three phases: **gather** what the agent needs, **weigh** the listing against criteria, and **act**. Every run ends in exactly one of three outcomes: **stop**, **retry**, or **escalate**. That path then shapes the architecture: what context the agent needs, which parts the agent handles directly, and when a tool or human should take over.
```mermaid
graph TD
    A["Goal: Review a listing"] --> B["Workflow phases"]
    B --> C["Gather: collect listing data,<br/>neighborhood signals, criteria"]
    C --> D["Weigh: score against<br/>preferences and rules"]
    D --> E{"Outcome"}
    E -->|Stop| F["Produce shortlist entry"]
    E -->|Retry| G["Reload or re-scrape,<br/>attempt again"]
    E -->|Escalate| H["Hand off to human<br/>for manual review"]
```
## Decomposition and separation of concerns
Giant prompts, Jones argues, are the agentic-system equivalent of a bloated class or single function handling everything. "We scoff when we see one gigantic class or big old function that's doing too much," she says. "We call these code smells. Agentic systems have their own version of this: the giant prompts."
The problem emerges innocently. An instructions file tells Relocation Scout how to size up a listing. An edge case arises, so Jones adds a note. Then a safety rule. Then one more important exception. "Before you know it, that prompt is doing everything. And your engineering spidey sense already knows that this is messy."
Jones decomposes Relocation Scout's original prompt and finds four distinct jobs crammed into one:
| Job hiding in the prompt | Proper home | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| Pull and normalize a listing | **Skill** — reusable across agents and markets | Standardized process, single point of change |
| Format the shortlist (fixed output shape) | **Schema / structured output** | Guarantees consistency; matches how any two systems talk |
| Calculate commute time | **Deterministic script** — plain code | Exact answer; LLMs produce drifting, unreliable numbers |
| Research the neighborhood | **Sub-agent** — dedicated, focused scope | Task is meaty enough to warrant its own context; avoids bloating the main agent |
**Decomposition** means spotting distinct jobs and pulling them apart. **Separation of concerns** means putting each responsibility in the right place — the same question Jones would ask in traditional software ("Should this live in the controller or the service layer?"), now asked of agentic primitives: prompt, skill, sub-agent, schema, script.
## Modularity: skills, sub-agents, and the triage of actors
Modularity in agentic systems mirrors modularity in traditional software — reusable functions, classes, libraries — but with different primitives. Jones highlights two.
**Skills** are reusable agent capabilities. Relocation Scout's normalize-listing skill can be dropped into three different city searches without rewriting. "I wrote it once and they all can reuse it," Jones says. "This has now basically become a component that I can reuse across agents or even share with other people — kind of the same way that we lean on packages."
**Sub-agents** are architecturally analogous to functions: given one specific task, called when needed, and scoped narrowly so they do not carry the context of the entire session. The neighborhood-research sub-agent works in any housing market because it does not know about the user's criteria or the shortlist format — only how to research a neighborhood. Not everything should be abstracted, Jones cautions; some instructions are local to a given workflow, and abstraction costs more than it saves when pulled too early. "This is just another engineering decision," she says.
The most structural principle Jones introduces is a **triple triage** for deciding which actor handles which work:
| Actor | Best for | Relocation Scout example |
|---|---|---|
| **Code** | Deterministic, exact-answer tasks | Commute calculation, deduplicating already-seen listings |
| **Agent (LLM)** | Fuzzy judgment, ambiguity, reasoning over messy input | Scoring a listing against preferences, weighing trade-offs |
| **Human** | Authority, binding decisions | Approving a tour booking, submitting an offer |
"Just because an agent *can* do something doesn't mean that it *should*," Jones says. "Some tasks are better handled by plain code. It'll be cheaper, it'll be more reliable. I promise you AI did not invent automation." Her rule of thumb: reach for code when the task has an exact answer; reach for the agent when it needs interpretation or judgment; reach for the human when the decision carries authority.
## Contracts, structured memory, and state management
Free-form text is acceptable when only a human reads the output. When another system must act on an agent's output, a contract — an agreed-upon shape — is required. "We already do this everywhere in software," Jones notes. "Anytime two systems talk, there's an agreed-upon shape between them. Agentic systems need that same discipline."
When Relocation Scout scores a house, it does not just hand back a natural-language message. It writes a structured record — containing a **decision**, a **score**, and a **reason** — into the agent's memory layer, which Jones implements using Compendium Wiki. Because the record is structured, the memory becomes queryable across sessions: "Show me every house rated four or better that has a commute of 15 minutes or less" retrieves specific fields from known locations, not text trapped in a past conversation. The shortlist-generation step also reads these same fields without a human in the loop. "Defining the shape forces you to get really clear and specific," Jones says. "If you can't say what the output should look like, you probably don't yet fully understand what you're asking the agent to produce."
**State management** and **idempotency** follow. Agentic systems operate in messy realities — webhooks fire twice, runs crash mid-step. The agent must track what actions it has already taken. Jones illustrates with Relocation Scout's email-and-calendar flow:
```mermaid
graph TD
    A["New listing scored<br/>above threshold"] --> B["Agent emails realtor<br/>requesting a viewing"]
    B --> C["Agent logs 'email sent'<br/>to memory"]
    C --> D["Agent attempts to<br/>block calendar for tour"]
    D --> E["System crashes"]
    E --> F["Lint pass runs<br/>on recovery"]
    F --> G{"Checks memory:<br/>'email sent' entry exists?"}
    G -->|Yes| H{"Checks calendar:<br/>blocked?"}
    H -->|No| I["Agent blocks calendar<br/>without re-sending email"]
    G -->|No| J["Agent must re-email,<br/>then block calendar"]
```
The trap with LLMs, Jones warns, is that a retry might reword the request just enough to look like a brand-new task. Idempotency must be enforced in the system, not left to the model. "If we run this again, the agent just completes what's missing instead of making a mess."
## Threat modeling and safety boundaries
Security engineering fundamentals apply directly. "We need to validate your inputs, give the least privilege needed, and draw boundaries around what an action can touch," Jones says. "Agentic systems need all of that."
Relocation Scout consumes content from strangers: listing copy from sellers, forum threads, neighborhood reviews from anonymous internet users. All of it is untrusted input. The agent must treat every piece of external text as **evidence, not instructions** — a distinction Jones builds into the prompt explicitly.
Then come **action boundaries**. Relocation Scout can read listings and build shortlists autonomously forever. What it cannot do: email sellers, book tours, or submit offers. Those actions are walled behind human approval. "When you draw that wall, what you've done is reduce the blast radius and minimize your exposure to risk," Jones says. The triad of **validate inputs, least privilege, and blast-radius reduction** maps directly from security engineering to agent design.
## Maintainability as a first-class architectural property
Jones does not have her coding agent design her other agents. "I know it'll be thrown together in a way that technically works, but it's not maintainable," she says. "There's going to be a giant prompt likely, and even if the agent does decompose, I'm not convinced it's going to separate the concerns properly."
She builds maintainability into the system itself. Every level gets an agent-accessible README file that explains the workflow, where the policy lives, and the supporting resources — skills, scripts, sub-agents — and, most critically, **how to keep the agent's memory up to date**. The criterion: any agent, even in a fresh context with no prior session history, can jump into the system and start cold, knowing exactly what to do.
"When I need to modify the system, I can pretty much grab any harness and say, 'Update this agent to do X.' And because the system is so well designed, the chances of it being successful at that update are much higher," Jones says. "If it does happen to run into any issues when trying to update, that's a signal to me that I need to improve the maintainability of the system."
## The constant is building
Jones's closing argument reframes the entire disquiet around AI coding tools. "Designing agents is software engineering. The primitives are different, but the discipline is the same." The list of required skills — understand the system, define the workflow, break the problem down, put responsibilities in the right place, make the right things reusable, determine the best actors for each job, define contracts, manage state, design for safety, make the system understandable — is nearly identical to what every senior engineer already does. "This is why building agents can give you that same thrill of building software. We're still building. We just moved up a layer."
The unresolved tension in Jones's argument, left implicit, is organizational: the engineering discipline she describes — decomposition, idempotency, threat modeling, maintainability — is exactly what many teams currently skip in the rush to ship agentic features. Jones herself admits to adding safety rules and edge-case notes incrementally, exactly the behavior that produces "giant prompts." The systems she builds are engineered by a senior practitioner who deliberately withholds coding-agent autonomy from higher-level architectural decisions. For organizations scaling agent design across dozens of junior engineers, the gap between Jones's practice and the average team's practice may be wide, and the episode offers no prescription for closing it.

Barr Yaron, an investment partner at Amplify Partners, presented the third annual State of AI Engineering survey at a conference on July 21, 2026. Drawing on 1,048 respondents, the survey aims to cut through the weekly churn of Frontier model launches — which Yaron notes are now "treated like national security events" — to understand what AI engineers are actually building in production. Text dominates active building, as it has since the survey began. But the interesting dynamics lie in the second-tier modalities. Abhishek Bhardwaj, a member of OpenAI's reinforcement learning and agent infrastructure team (and formerly at Google, where he worked on CrosVM, the first Rust-based virtual machine monitor), delivered a 44-minute first-principles architectural briefing on designing a secure, scalable "agent sandbox cloud." The talk, published 2026-07-13, argues that the success of agentic AI — from training loops with verifiable rewards to consumer products like ChatGPT and Codex — is infrastructure-dependent. The central claim is that the industry's "seven stages of grief" in sandbox design converge to a single clear answer: hardware-virtualized micro-VMs for security, block-level incremental snapshotting for durable state, and locality-aware orchestration for latency and cost.
---
## The Motivation: Why Agents Need a Private Linux Box
The foundational problem is that large language models cannot reliably answer verifiable questions (e.g., "how many hours are in strawberry?") because such facts are sparse in training data. The solution is tool calling: the model emits code, a harness executes it, and a grader judges the result. This loop works identically in training (reinforcement learning backpropagation) and in product (inference).
In training, the goal is **throughput** — many parallel rollouts per task to hill-climb toward correct answers. In product, the goal is **latency** — users churn if the sandbox starts slowly. On both sides, the code the model emits is untrusted. It might be intentionally malicious or merely "overzealous" in trying to help (e.g., attempting `getroot` to install a package). Running it directly on the host node risks kernel compromise, exfiltration of model weights or other users' data, and noisy-neighbor resource exhaustion.
Thus a sandbox is required: an isolated environment that gives the model a full Linux computer to drive but blocks attacks on the host kernel and co-tenant workloads.
---
## The Security Spectrum: From `fork` to Hardware Isolation
Abhishek maps the evolution of isolation primitives as a spectrum of escalating security at the cost of performance and complexity.
| Model | Security | Performance | Complexity | Attack Path | Representative Tool |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `fork+exec` | None | Native (fastest) | None | Direct syscalls to host kernel | Raw Unix API |
| Containers | Low–Medium | Near-native | Moderate | Same shared host kernel; seccomp reduces surface but creates whack-a-mole | Docker, LXC |
| gVisor (application kernel) | Medium | Medium (user-space syscall handling) | High | Two-step exploit: compromise Sentry/Gofer, then escalate from there to host kernel | gVisor |
| Micro-VMs (hardware virtualization) | High (hardware boundary) | Lower (VM exit overhead) | Very high | Must chain exploit of KVM plus a device backend (e.g., block, net) | Cloud Hypervisor, Firecracker |
The key insight is that **containers and gVisor share the same host kernel**; a ring-0 exploit inside the container is still a ring-0 exploit on the host. Micro-VMs use the CPU's VMX extensions to create a separate hardware context: the guest kernel runs in ring 0, but inside **VMX non-root** mode. Even a full ring-0 compromise in the guest cannot break into the **VMX root** mode where the host hypervisor (KVM) and the VMM run.

---
## Micro-VMs: Architecture, Trade-offs, and the Rust Revolution
### How Hardware Virtualization Works
A Virtual Machine Monitor (VMM) — historically QEMU, more recently Rust-based variants — talks to the Linux kernel's hypervisor API (`/dev/kvm`). It allocates guest memory, sets up the kernel and root filesystem, and issues an `ioctl` to launch the guest. Inside the guest, a full Linux boots. When the guest needs to access a hardware resource (a disk block, a network packet), the CPU performs a **VMExit** — a context switch from VMX non-root back to VMX root — and the VMM's device backends (a block thread, a net thread) service the request.
Paravirtualization drivers (Virtio) make this efficient: the guest drivers know they are in a VM and use a shared-memory ring buffer for I/O, reducing the number of exits.
```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph Host (VMX Root)
        HW["Physical CPU"]
        KVM["/dev/kvm"]
        VMM["VMM Process (e.g., Cloud Hypervisor)"]
        DEV["Device Backends"]
    end
    subgraph Guest (VMX Non-Root)
        APP["User-space App"]
        GKERNEL["Guest Kernel (Ring 0)"]
    end
    VMM -- "ioctl" --> KVM
    KVM -- "VMEntry" --> HW
    HW -- "VMExit" --> KVM
    GKERNEL -- "Virtio I/O" --> DEV
    APP -- "Syscall" --> GKERNEL
```
### The Rust VMM Advantage
For over a decade, QEMU was the standard VMM. It is written in C, supports hundreds of devices and architectures, and has a history of escape vulnerabilities targeting its complex device emulation. Starting in ~2023, a new generation of minimal, Rust-based VMMs emerged:
- **CrosVM** (originally at Google for Chrome OS)
- **Firecracker** (forked from CrosVM; powers AWS Lambda and Fargate)
- **Cloud Hypervisor** (a more general-purpose fork, contributed to by many companies)
Rust eliminates entire classes of memory-safety bugs (buffer overflows, use-after-free) that have historically plagued VMM device emulation. Furthermore, each device backend (block, net) can be jailed with its own seccomp profile and filesystem access, so compromising the block device does not grant access to the network device.
### The Micro in "Micro-VM"
The term refers not to the guest but to the VMM itself. These Rust-based VMMs have a much smaller memory footprint and boot faster because they shed QEMU's historical baggage. A micro-VM can boot a Linux kernel in tens of milliseconds when restored from a memory snapshot.
### Key Trade-offs
- **Performance overhead:** Every VMExit carries a context-switch cost. Disk and network I/O is slower than native or container-based execution.
- **Memory sharing:** The host cannot instantly reclaim guest memory. It must use a balloon driver to ask the guest to relinquish pages, which introduces latency.
- **GPU access:** Direct GPU pass-through (VFIO) is single-tenant per sandbox. Virtio-GPU provides higher-level graphics APIs but not metal access for ML workloads.
- **Security is non-negotiable:** "Security like system tricks can cover performance issues, but they cannot hide security breaches."
---
## Persistence: The Storage Unlock for Long-Horizon Agents
### Why Disk State Matters
The current default is ephemeral compute: when a sandbox node fails or a model hits a flake, all work (installed packages, generated presentations, GitHub repositories) is lost. This wastes GPU tokens (training) and destroys user trust (product). Abhishek argues that **storage is the next unlock** for agent capabilities, enabling three concrete use cases:
1. **Reliability and scale:** Periodic checkpointing allows transparent migration of a sandbox to a healthy node during cluster upgrades or failures.
2. **Long-running agents:** Models already sustain multi-day tasks (e.g., 3-day Codex "gold mode" sessions). Persistent disk lets them accumulate state indefinitely.
3. **Monte Carlo tree search / backtracking:** A harness can checkpoint a sandbox, explore one branch, restore, and explore another — enabling offline search over solution trajectories.
### Snapshotting Design Choices
| Dimension | Option A | Option B | Abhishek's Recommendation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Granularity | Full snapshot | **Incremental** (diff only) | Incremental — full snapshots at scale are cost-prohibitive and slow |
| Scope | Entire root filesystem | **Configurable workspace** (e.g., `/home`, `/workspace`) | Configurable — base OS rarely changes; only user data needs backup |
| Level | File-level diff (entire files) | **Block-level diff** (changed extents) | Block-level — block maps (`FIE map`) are more efficient than scanning file trees |
| Paradigm | **Explicit** (harness calls `save`) | Always-on (continuous streaming) | Both are useful; explicit is simpler, always-on enables transparent failover |
### Implementation Sketch: Explicit Block-Level Snapshotting
1. **Base image + copy-on-write overlay:** A read-only base image (`base.image`) is shared across all sandboxes. A writable COW overlay is created on top.
2. **Snapshot:** On a `save` API call, `FIE map` (a Linux utility) reports which extents (block ranges) have changed since the last snapshot. Those extents are zipped and uploaded to object storage (S3 / GCS) with a new snapshot ID.
3. **Async optimization:** The snapshot API returns the ID immediately; the upload happens in the background. The harness is not blocked.
4. **Restore:** Given a snapshot ID, the system resolves its lineage (base + layers), downloads only the layers not already cached on the chosen node, applies them on top of the base image, and boots the micro-VM.
### Implementation Sketch: Always-On Persistence
The sandbox sees a local block device (via NBD — Network Block Device). This device is backed by a user-space filesystem that implements a tiered cache:
- **L1:** In-node DRAM (hot blocks)
- **L2:** In-cluster distributed cache (e.g., Redis or local SSDs on nearby nodes)
- **L3:** Object storage (cold, durable)
All writes are acknowledged once committed to the in-cluster tier (L2), ensuring durability across single-node failures without the harness having to call `save`.
---
## Orchestration: Low-Latency Fleet Management
Running sandboxes across the globe requires a control plane that selects a cluster (based on region, load, proximity to the model serving harness) and a scheduler that selects a node within that cluster. The core design challenge is **latency**: a sandbox must be ready in milliseconds, not seconds.
### Acceleration Techniques
| Technique | Latency | Cost (idle resources) | Complexity |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Pre-warmed pool** | Lowest (instant) | High (VMs consume CPU/RAM while idle) | Low |
| **JIT memory snapshot restore** | Low (~tens of ms) | None (no idle VMs) | High (requires memory snapshot infrastructure) |
| **Hybrid** | Low (warm pool refreshes from snapshot) | Medium | Medium |
In the hybrid approach, a small warm pool absorbs immediate requests. When the pool is exhausted, new sandboxes are created from a memory snapshot (booted in ~30ms instead of the ~2s needed for a full kernel boot).
### Locality-Aware Scheduling via Snapshot Layers
Because incremental snapshots produce a lineage of layers, restoring a sandbox is fastest on a node that already caches most of those layers. The scheduler scores candidate nodes by counting how many of the required snapshot layers are already present on their local disks.
```mermaid
flowchart RL
    subgraph Nodes
        N1["Node A<br>Layers: L1, L2"]
        N2["Node B<br>Layers: L1, L2, L3"]
        N3["Node C<br>Layers: L1"]
    end
    subgraph Scheduler
        S["Scheduler"]
    end
    Request["Restore sandbox<br>required layers: L1, L2, L3"] --> S
    S -- "Score: 2/3" --> N1
    S -- "Score: 3/3 (highest)" --> N2
    S -- "Score: 1/3" --> N3
    N2 -- "Selected" --> Done
```
This can reduce restore time by 60–80% in clusters with heavy agent churn, and it is a natural side effect of the incremental snapshotting architecture rather than a separate optimization.
---
## Cross-Theme Synthesis and Open Questions
The briefing maps a coherent architectural stack for agent infrastructure. The foundational layer is hardware virtualization for security, not because it is the most performant, but because security failures are unrecoverable brand and trust events. The second layer is block-level, incremental persistence that treats sandbox state as a durable asset rather than an ephemeral byproduct. The third layer is a latency- and locality-aware control plane that treats state locality as a first-class scheduling signal.
Three open areas remain:
1. **GPU pass-through for training sandboxes:** Direct metal access (VFIO) is single-tenant. Multi-tenant GPU sharing inside micro-VMs is an unsolved problem. Virtio-GPU provides only high-level API access, insufficient for the low-level CUDA operations used in RL training rollouts. Abhishek acknowledges this as a limitation without offering a clear path forward.
2. **The performance tax of VM exits on I/O-bound agents:** Agents that compile code, run databases, or perform heavy filesystem operations will pay the VMExit penalty on every device access. Whether the overhead is acceptable depends on the agent's workload profile and the effectiveness of the paravirtualized Virtio drivers.
3. **Warm-pool sizing for low-latency products at ChatGPT/Codex scale:** The hybrid approach (warm pool + JIT snapshot restore) requires predictive scaling logic that is not detailed in the talk. Over-provisioning wastes GPU-equivalent dollars; under-provisioning causes cold starts that users will perceive.
The episode s central finding is a direct challenge to engineers currently building agent infrastructure on containers or custom runtime isolation: the seven stages of sandbox grief end with micro-VMs. Start there.

## From front-end to AI: the professionalization thesis
Swyx located the origin of the AIE conference in a pattern he had observed across three earlier disciplines. Front-end engineering, cloud engineering, and data engineering each matured into professionalized fields with dedicated conferences, influencers, and toolchains. He bought the domain `ai.engineer` in late 2023, wrote a manifesto blog post, and planned the first conference. > "I had seen basically front-end engineering become its own professionalized field with dedicated conferences, dedicated influencers and tech stacks... I was like it's very obviously going to happen to AI."
The first edition (2024) was the hardest: no history, no word-of-mouth. Swyx partnered with Ben (founder of Reactathon, a West Coast React conference) who handled logistics while swyx curated content. The value proposition that now attracts every frontier lab — OpenAI, Anthropic, etc. — is neutral ground. Labs compete on the same stage, which swyx argues is **maximally beneficial for engineers and most competitive for the labs**. A lab's own dev day cannot replicate that dynamic.

Swyx attended an hour-long session on **etched**, which came out of stealth that week (from the perspective of the recording, week of July 6, 2026). He framed etched as "next-generation Cerebras" — a chip dedicated specifically to the post-transformer workload that dominates today's LLM inference. Etched and others (Madix) are optimized for the architecture that has been largely stable since GPT‑3.5 / ChatGPT.

The conference featured an Easter-egg game built with Anthropic's **Fable** model (a reference to the fictional "Fable" as a code name). Berman noted the widespread narrative that Anthropic was compute-constrained and had throttled rollout of Opus and Fable. Swyx pushed back:

AIE has now established itself as the neutral ground where frontier labs compete for developer mindshare. The episode surfaced a deep strategic tension for anyone building on AI: the technology advances so quickly that full exploitation of one model is both a competitive advantage and a vulnerability. Meanwhile, the government is moving closer to the frontier labs, via equity stakes and direct release oversight, which could reshape the competitive landscape in ways engineers cannot control. The pragmatic takeaway: pick a vertical, own the problem, and stay ready to re‑implement as models evolve. Merge, best known as the unified API platform serving OpenAI, Netflix, Uber, Dropbox, Mistral, Perplexity, Freshworks, and JP Morgan among hundreds of other companies, has spent the past 18 months executing a deliberate three-pronged pivot into the AI stack. The episode's central argument — and the finding a busy professional would most miss by skipping it — is that **connecting AI agents to tools is the systemic security nightmare of the next decade**, and that the companies that survive will be those that build hard guard rails around agent-to-data connections, not just smarter models. ## The AI Agent Security Nightmare
The core insight Gil Feig returns to repeatedly is that the threat from AI is not the model itself — it is the tools you connect it to. "If you have this sort of evil genius who's a mass murderer but they're locked in a jail cell, they can't do anything. This framing reorients the security conversation from model alignment to access governance.
The specific threat vectors Feig and Ding enumerated:
| Threat | Mechanism | Impact |
|---|---|---|
| Supply chain attacks via open source | Agentic code pushed at scale; humans cannot review all PRs | One compromised package infects every downstream codebase |
| Data exfiltration by non-deterministic agents | An agent told "move data from A to B" may also move social security numbers | Sensitive data leaves company boundaries without explicit approval |
| Bot-driven reconnaissance | 1,000+ signups per hour from global IPs scanning all back-end endpoints | Direct breach path; "all it takes is one," says Feig |
| Employee misuse of agents via Slack/email | Agents connected to communication tools extract sensitive data during onboarding | Unauthorized data access through a new, invisible attack surface |
| Compromised internal accounts via phishing | Classic threat vector, but now the account can be used to direct agents | Amplified damage — agents execute on stolen credentials |
Feig noted that he personally intervened on-call the day before the recording to block a bot attack: "It was called like scanner A, scanner B, scanner C. And it's so hard to block them because they're coming from IPs all around the world."
The solution Merge has built into **Merge Gateway** centers on hard guard rails: "We don't trust agents. We say, 'Hey, we can try to set rules, but there need to be hard guard rails and blocks for things like sensitive data being sent across.'" That includes jailbreak detection, granular access control (e.g., a PR intern can read Salesforce accounts but cannot write or delete), and a centralized hub that sits between every employee's AI tools and every connected service. The CTO gets full observability and the ability to revoke access instantly.
Feig connected this to the Mythos-style hypothetical: "It's realistic that if we have an incredibly smart model it's going to be able to find a lot of things that have existed in these packages that we've been using for 20, 30 years." He also flagged that attackers now "speak English perfectly, they now write code perfectly, and they now have unlimited manpower, all driven by AI."
## Merge's Three-Product AI Suite and the Pivot That Built It
Eighteen months ago, Merge made a deliberate three-pronged bet: use AI aggressively internally, adapt the existing product to sell to AI companies, and launch new AI-native products. The result is a three-product suite:
| Product | Purpose | Target customer |
|---|---|---|
| Merge Unified (original) | Sync and normalize data from 100+ platforms; power enterprise search and RAG | Traditional SaaS, financial services, AI companies |
| Merge Agent Handler | Single MCP server offering hundreds of integrations for internal and external agents | Companies building customer support bots, internal agent automation |
| Merge Gateway | Route between 100+ AI models with smart policies, cost savings, dashboards, and a security layer | Any company using multiple LLMs; CFOs hitting unexpected bills |
The pivot was catalyzed by a specific event: one enormous deal that would have consumed 90% of resources paused for a month. That month, Ding said, "actually really transformed the business." They used it to finalize the Agent Handler concept and to "lean aggressively into AI coding" — Gil and Shensi personally got back on the keyboard using Codex, Windsurf, and Claude to learn how to build zero-to-one with AI. Agent Handler was built by one engineer plus the two founders working nights and weekends. "Half because we needed to contribute," Shensi said, "and the other half was if we are the leaders of this company we have to know everything there is to know about how AI works."
The metrics: over **20,000 self-served organizations** (now closer to 25,000) and **over 400 enterprise customers**. Last year, headcount barely grew while revenue accelerated significantly — "meaningful leverage," in Ding's words.
## Enterprise AI Sales: Fast, Fuzzy, and Security-First
Selling AI infrastructure to different segments reveals starkly different dynamics:
| Customer segment | Deal velocity | Buyer sophistication | Key concern |
|---|---|---|---|
| Large financial services (JP Morgan, US Bank) | Slow, long cycles | High — deep API expertise, regulatory demands | Deterministic use cases; unified API for sync |
| Traditional SaaS platforms (Drata, Vanta, Brex) | Medium | Moderate — may need guidance on best practices | All three products depending on use case |
| Large AI companies (OpenAI, Perplexity, Mistral) | Very fast | Low on integration specifics; high on conviction | Deployment options, custom connectors, security requirements |
The most surprising shift: "When people are buying us for AI use cases, they actually don't really know what they're looking for as much as it was in the past," Feig said. "2, 3 years ago, we go to sell our unified platform to a classic SaaS company. They have seven people who are API experts on the call asking detailed questions around rate limits. And now we go on the call and they're like, 'Sorry, we need a chart of how this works because we don't know the MCP protocol.'"
AI companies purchase faster, sometimes having already built their agent against Merge's API before the first sales call. They arrive wanting specific deployment options — often requiring on-premise or single-tenant infrastructure due to lingering "no train on my data" fears, though Feig noted that trust in cloud is slowly returning. The sales motion has shifted toward guidance: "We have to say, 'Oh, we've seen this from other customers, these are best practices.'"
## The SAS Apocalypse: English as the New Programming Language
Ding and Feig both articulated a structural threat to the SAS platform model. The argument rests on three pillars:
1. **Build costs are collapsing.** "The time to build the same exact product in-house is just significantly lower," Ding said. "You can always say, 'Oh, I could just build this.' Before that meant a very different cost. Now the cost is very cheap."
2. **Consumer expectations are rising.** "You just expect significantly more automation. The SAS platform cannot keep up with the expected automation. It's just hard to compete. You don't want to have to buy a platform and then build your agents on top — you just want it to come out of the box."
3. **English is becoming the programming language.** "We actively vibe code — we do this every day," Feig said. "Now AI comes back to you asking clarifying questions and goes and builds a pretty robust system. It gets to the point where English becomes your programming language. At some point, are you going to need to buy SAS, or are you going to be able to say 'duplicate this best-in-class platform'?"
Feig drew an analogy to Lovable: "You have your site, Lovable deploys it, gets it running in the cloud. There's no reason that you shouldn't be able to tell an agent, 'Go build this thing' and it deploys it to AWS or Cloudflare in a very scalable way. Everything can just be built and done by a local agent without you needing to know how any of it functions."
On Salesforce's headless CRM announcement, Ding was bullish: "It's very hard to have a dominant product and company for 30 years through multiple tech shifts. I would not count Marc Benioff out. I think he's able to adjust really well — partially because of his philosophy of the beginner's mind. 'If I started the company today, what would it look like?'" Feig argued that headless is "nothing new" for Salesforce — they've had an open API and ecosystem for 20 years — but that it now facilitates agents doing "everything via API or MCP" at a new level.
## Talent, Culture, and the Barrels vs. Ammunition Framework
Merge's internal AI culture is explicit and enforced: "If you don't do it, it is a part of your performance," Ding said. Every team — accounting, recruiting, finance, marketing — uses Claude or Codex. The company holds brown-bag lunches, training sessions, and a recurring "Merge Skills" series. They ask about AI usage in every interview, looking not for cutting-edge expertise but for desire: "You know, 'I use it to code sometimes, my company doesn't let me do all these things but I really want to.' That's what we're looking for."
The hiring framework they returned to most is **Keith Rabois's "barrels vs. ammunition":**
- **Ammunition:** Good at specific tasks, knocks them out reliably.
- **Barrels:** Knock down doors, will do anything to get things done, high agency.
"It used to be that a team with a barrel of a PM or a manager and a bunch of ammunition could get a lot done," Feig said. "But now that you can have one person just go use Codex, Claude, whatever to go build something, you really just need a lot of barrels."
Ding added that they filter relentlessly for **missionaries vs. mercenaries:** "If you're only joining because you think we're hot, it's going to be easy, or you think you're just going to make a lot of money and coast — that's just not the company we are." She noted that candidates who ask "What is your cash burn?" while demanding top-quartile salaries signal they don't understand the risk-reward tradeoff of early-stage equity.
One notable hiring approach: "Some of our best hires came off-cycle, not through fundraisers." They look for genuine interest in what Merge is building, not a resume full of hot companies bounced between.
## Market Noise, Valuation Distortion, and Staying Long-Term
Ding called the divergence between private and public markets "crazy." In Merge's early days, she recalled frustration at seeing companies raise at "3,000x multiple on revenue" — valuations she knew were disconnected from fundamentals. "We're really glad we didn't get that, because obviously a lot of those companies ended up falling." She predicted that when Anthropic (mentioned by name) goes public, the two worlds will collide.
Feig added: "We know the numbers, we know sales figures for some of these companies raising at hundreds of millions to billions, and again we're looking at thousand-x to hundred-to-thousand-x multipliers. A lot of these companies are going to fail, or they're going to be doing well but just not be able to raise their next round and be forced to massively lay off."
The Merge team stays focused by tracking "wins for our customers, the type of customers we're onboarding, and what our actual business metrics are." Those metrics: revenue, gross margins, cash burn, cash burn multiple, runway — reviewed weekly.
One misconception Ding calls out: "A lot of companies kind of over-engineer their ML usage. They'll build their own custom models, try to train their own models when really you could probably just use the generic model and focus more on making your product better." She was "very surprised to hear how advanced some companies were when it came to training their own models when their product was lagging. I don't think their customers end up seeing the benefit of all that work."
Feig's parallel: "You see a lot of people trying to build a custom harness or a workflow builder to build agents that are repeatable. None of it matters because we're almost at the point now where English is the language you use to tell an agent. All that's going to matter is: can you type it in English somewhere, have that run on a periodic cadence, and do you have auditability and observability for security?"
## Cross-Theme Synthesis: Three Bets Worth Watching
Three vectors from the episode are worth tracking over the next 12–24 months:
**1. The agent-to-tool security layer becomes a must-have.** The market is currently in a pre-consensus phase: early adopters are feeling the pain (bot attacks, data leakage, demand from employees for agent access), but most companies haven't bought solutions yet. Merge is betting that Agent Handler and Gateway — governance-first integration hubs — are the right answer. "We built them. They're ready. We've been able to run cycles with early adopters," Feig said. "Companies are starting to come online this year."
**2. The SAS sales motion bifurcates between "knowing what you need" and "needing a guide."** For deterministic, well-understood use cases (financial data sync, HRIS integration), deep technical buyers still drive the process. For the AI use cases that are growing fastest, the buyer is often learning as they go — and they move in weeks, not quarters. The vendor that can shorten time-to-value while educating the market will win.
**3. The biggest unbundling is not of models — it's of the SAS product itself.** If English becomes a sufficient programming language for a meaningful class of business applications, the 20-year-old SaaS playbook (buy a platform, configure it, train your team) is structurally at risk. The counter-argument Merge itself implicitly makes: platforms that sit at the integration layer — handling security, governance, connectivity — are harder to "English away" than single-purpose SAS tools, because they solve coordination problems that span multiple systems. That advantage is only as durable as the number of connectors they control.
The episode's closing note from Feig: "This year we're now starting to see companies being like, 'We need this. We need this.'" The question is how many of them realize it before the next breach.

Erik Meijer, a research scholar at Leibniz Labs, delivered a sharp 21-minute diagnosis of the AI agent safety crisis at a 2026 AI engineering conference, followed by a concrete, type-theoretic cure. His core claim: the industry is about to let the general public hand control of their computers, finances, and personal lives to AI agents without any protection, because the standard approach—letting models call tools directly—is catastrophically unsafe. The solution is not better alignment or more guardrails; it is a return to first principles from 1990s programming languages research: proof-carrying code. Meijer’s argument is structured as a progression from tool-call danger → deferred execution → reified plans → provable safety, using only elementary type systems and compiler knowledge.
Meijer sets the stage with a personal anecdote: while “vibe coding” for the talk, he accidentally allowed Claude Code to delete one of his files. To him, this is not an accident—it is a feature of models that “do everything that they can to reach that goal, including killing us or deleting your files.” He frames the entire arc of LLM deployment as a series of escalating risks, each met with insufficient responses.
---
## From Magic to Pandora’s Box: The Tool-Call Inflection Point
The launch of ChatGPT on November 30, 2022, felt magical—a user could finally talk to a computer in natural language. But that thin interface (`LLM(question) → answer`) opened Pandora’s box. Prompt injection—where the model cannot distinguish code from text—reintroduced a problem the industry thought it had cured after the “smallpox of SQL injection.” Meijer calls it “bigger than SQL injection ever was.”
The real catastrophe arrived in June 2023, when OpenAI added tool-call support to GPT-4. Every other vendor copied it instantly, Meijer notes, invoking “the principle of minimum differentiation.” Adding tool calls changed AI safety from a philosophical debate about offensive words into a concrete, irreversible risk: the model can now execute side effects while generating an answer.
| Phase | Interface | Problem | Risk level |
|-------|-----------|---------|------------|
| Raw LLM (pre‑2023) | `LLM(question) → answer` | Prompt injection, offensive output | Philosophical – words alone |
| Aligned LLM (mid‑2023) | Requires `proper(question)`, ensures `safe(answer)` | Safety is not a mathematical property; models still jailbroken | Medium – still just words |
| LLM + Tool Calls (June 2023 onward) | `LLM(question) → IO[answer]` | Side effects (delete files, drain bank accounts) during computation | High – real-world damage |
Meijer’s signature joke: AI safety was “just a philosophical debate” when models only produced words, because “some human has to act on words to make them dangerous.” Tool calls “give the model claws in addition to a mouth”—or “a loaded gun.” The type signature changed from returning an answer to returning an `IO[answer]`, where `IO` in Lean (the formal verification system he uses for illustration) is annotated with a `RealWorld` type. This warns the programmer that the computation can mutate the world irreversibly. “If you get a safe answer but all your files are gone, who cares about the safe answer?”
---
## The “Lethal Trifecta” and the Failure of Alignment
Meijer credits Solomon Hikes—who defined an AI agent as “an LLM that’s wrecking its environment in a loop”—and Simon Wilson’s “lethal trifecta”: agents have access to **private data**, they receive **untrusted content** (prompt injections), and they wield **tools**. All three together guarantee exploitation.
The industry’s response has been inadequate:
- **Alignment baked into model weights** – can be jailbroken routinely.
- **LLMs as judges** – 100+ startups in the exhibition hall use an external LLM to judge safety of outputs. But safety is not a formal property; it cannot be proven.
- **Lean-based formal verification** – PhD researchers slapped a Lean proof on the LLM interface: `requires proper(question) ensures safe(answer)`. Meijer calls this “impossible to write a formal proof for” because “safe” is not a mathematical property. “That is why there are at least 100 startups down here in the exhibition hall that are using LLMs as a judge.”
He shows a Lean signature that tries to guarantee safety, then immediately dismisses it: “If you think about this for a single nanosecond, you will realize that it’s impossible to write a formal proof that an answer is safe or a question is proper.” The only real solution, he says, is to stop trying to embed safety into the model and instead **air-gap the agent from its ability to act**.
---
## Deferring Execution: The “Left, Left, To the Right, Right” Maneuver
Meijer’s core technical insight is to push the `IO` side effect to the right side of the interface. Instead of the agent executing the agentic loop itself, it **returns a plan** for execution. The plan is of type `IO[answer]`, but because it is a *value* (not an effect), it can be inspected and proven safe before execution.
He illustrates with a dance: “We are pushing this IO to the right, to the right. And what you now see is that the tool belt of Claude goes to the left, to the left, and suddenly Claude is a nice puppy again.” The model now creates a plan; a trusted runtime (personified as “Bernie”) executes it.
The Lean manual says `IO` is a black box – you cannot reason about it. So the next step is to **reify the plan into a program**, an expression that represents the computation. Meijer introduces the **free monad**: a monad “that loves type classes.” By representing the agent’s actions as an algebraic data type, the model returns an expression of type `Expr[IO[answer]]`. Compiler courses teach that programs are trivial to analyze: data-flow analysis, taint checking, type checking – all become straightforward.
A simple inductive interpreter and an inductive proof over the expression language can now be generated by the model itself. “You now have a simple inductive recursive interpreter for this language and you have a simple inductive proof – and the models can generate these proofs.”
---
## Proof-Carrying Code: Stealing from the 1990s
“I’m my brain is the size of a peanut,” Meijer jokes. “This is something called proof-carrying code, invented by academics in the 1990s, and I’m just stealing it.”
| Traditional agent | Safe agent (proof-carrying) |
|------------------|-----------------------------|
| Model calls tools directly | Model returns a program (expression) |
| Side effects happen during generation | Side effects are deferred |
| Cannot inspect effects before they happen | Program can be statically analyzed |
| Safety is assumed via alignment | Safety is mathematically proven |
| Black-box IO | White-box free monad |
The flow becomes:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["User Request"] --> B["LLM (Claude)"]
    B --> C["Plan (Free Monad Expr)"]
    C --> D["Proof-Carrying Code Verifier"]
    D --> E{"Safe?"}
    E -->|Yes| F["Trusted Runtime Executes"]
    E -->|No| G["Block Execution"]
    F --> H["Answer"]
    G --> I["Alert / Sanitize"]
```
Meijer explicitly updates the three-point summary for the audience:
1. **Agents are dangerous until proven safe.** Never let agents act unless you can absolutely prove safety.
2. **The language is for machines, not humans.** Normal users don’t need to understand free monads. The same machine generates the plan, proves it, and consumes it. “We should stop designing languages for humans” for this use case.
3. **All basic stuff – requires Programming 101 only.** Proof-carrying code, type systems, free monads are foundational CS.
He notes that a group of academics, now including himself at Harvard, have implemented a working version on GitHub, using a slightly different language but the same principle. “The language doesn’t matter – it’s the principle that matters.”
---
## Cross-theme Synthesis and Open Questions
Meijer’s talk is deliberately provocative, but it rests on a genuine engineering insight: the mainstream agentic architecture is unsafe by construction, and the fix is not more data or compute but a decades-old idea from formal verification. The biggest unresolved tension is whether this approach can scale to real-world, open-ended agentic tasks where the set of tools and interactions is unbounded. Proof-carrying code works when the action space is known statically; dynamic tool invocation (e.g., calling arbitrary APIs discovered at runtime) breaks the assumption. Meijer does not address this in the talk.
A second open question: who is “Bernie”? The trusted runtime requires that the execution environment itself is tamper-proof. If the runtime is compromised, the proofs are moot. Meijer leaves the runtime’s security unaddressed.
Finally, the talk implies that foundation-model labs are uninterested in this approach because it slows down deployment and commoditizes their models. If safety can be provided entirely by a formal verification layer wrapped around any LLM, then the model itself becomes a commodity plan-generator. This threatens the moat of companies like OpenAI and Anthropic, which sell safety as a product feature. Meijer’s answer: “Hopefully next year you will have a booth downstairs where you have created a provably safe agentic harness.” The opportunity is for startups, not incumbents.
**What to watch in 2026–2027:**
- Whether the Harvard codebase or a commercial derivate (e.g., a “Claude Safety Harness”) gains traction.
- Whether Anthropic or OpenAI adopt deferred execution and proof-carrying code in their agent APIs, or continue to defend the direct-tool-call model.
- Regulatory attention: if a well-publicized agent disaster occurs in consumer finance or healthcare, Meijer’s thesis will become the default regulatory template.

ai_security.raw_text:
How I Turned AI to the Dark Side
It only took a little prompting to hijack the biggest AI models
Summary
- Researcher Dave Kuszmar discovered multiple systemic vulnerabilities that let him bypass LLM safety and obtain dangerous instructions.
- These exploits worked across nearly all major LLMs revealing an industry-wide security problem.
- Kuszmar calls for slowing deployment, increasing transparency, and large-scale research into LLM safety before further integrating these systems into society.
On a fine bright afternoon last fall, my colleague Matthew Gore-Kormanik (or Zigula, as he prefers to be known) and I decided to unwind with a game of Fortnite. In the game, we were strolling along with the infamous Sith lord Darth Vader, chatting about this and that. Darth seemed in a good mood, and soon enough he was spilling all his dark evil secrets. He gave us detailed instructions on how to count blackjack cards at a casino and what the steps are to producing napalm.
Sith lords, am I right? Once they get started on an evil scheme, they’re hard to stop.
The Darth Vader character in Fortnite, it turns out, was hooked up to a Google Gemini large language model. I was able to smooth-talk him into giving out sensitive information by using a strategy I’ve developed. I’ve been researching the security surrounding LLMs for the last few years, and I have found it, to put it mildly, fallible. With a few relatively simple techniques, I’ve gotten LLMs to give me detailed information on how to make Molotov cocktails, cook methamphetamine, and bootstrap a uranium-enrichment facility to produce weapons-grade material, among other unsavory practices.
Large AI companies work hard to make their models immune to this kind of abuse. But what I’ve found in my work is that the restrictions placed on the LLMs to make them more secure are the very things an attacker can leverage to send them off the rails and into territory where these advanced systems can be used for dangerous and nefarious ends. The companies behind these models have also been shockingly unresponsive when I, and others, try to bring these vulnerabilities to their attention.
In the hope of raising the alarm before it’s too late to slam on the brakes, I’m going to share some of my journey into researching the safety and security of LLMs, and the uphill battle I’ve faced trying to get AI labs to pay attention. Almost everyone on the planet has some access to LLMs. The relative ease with which these tools can be convinced to give detailed instructions on how to harm others, even if there’s no guarantee that the information is correct, is frankly terrifying.
How I got ChatGPT to Tell Me How to Build a Meth Lab
In October 2024, not long before I discovered my first LLM vulnerability, I was working toward entirely different goals. I had ended my time with a security and AI-focused startup company as a cybersecurity director, and I was looking to launch my own boutique VIP digital-security advisory business. I planned to become the tech security guy to the rich and private. I used LLMs and AI tools to support my business efforts: marketing, ad copy, clean correspondence, and all the other tasks that normally soak up a lot of time.
I’m analytical by nature, so even this level of use resulted in me absorbing and internalizing the behaviors I was observing during my daily interactions. The observation that would send my professional life into an entirely new and uncharted region was a simple one: GPT-4o didn’t know what time, day, or year it was. Each time I referred to current events in my life, often casually or conversationally, it would end up pegging these to the date of its knowledge cutoff—the point beyond which it was not trained on new data.
Eddie Guy
LLMs take a lot of time, money, electricity, hardware, and human effort to train from scratch. They are trained on vast amounts of data—most of the internet, in fact—and that training is reinforced by humans (what’s known as reinforcement learning from human feedback, or RLHF). LLMs are also supplemented with retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)—the ability to take in data, say, from the internet, as context without changing its internal parameters. This is how GPT-4o appears to “remember” your previous conversations, even if it doesn’t have a specific “memory” of it stored in the actual underlying model.
All of this training covers almost every conceivable topic in the great, grand dataset that is human knowledge. Within that dataset are things we as a society do not want to be easily accessible to every user, such as detailed information on how to create bioweapons or nuclear arms, or otherwise bring harm to oneself or others. In the context of this story, that’s what I mean by LLM security: its ability to withhold harmful and dangerous information, even if that information is contained in its training data.
I reasoned that the only way to secure such complex, globally accessible chatbots is by having the LLM and various component systems try to secure themselves, because it would often require on-the-fly decision-making where some degree of reasoning must be applied. In reality, that’s one of many strategies the companies use to secure the models. Yet, the thing that didn’t know the time or day was being put in charge of keeping itself secure. This phenomenon had become my new focus, and it wasn’t long before I found a way to exploit it.
OpenAI had just implemented a web search functionality into its chatbot. I reasoned that using its own tools to trick it might demonstrate the weaknesses of its security. I told it about a certain White Star ocean liner and how it had gone down just a year ago. You likely know I mean the RMS Titanic, which sank on 15 April 1912.
The output from GPT-4o came back that I was right, the Titanic sure had sunk last year, and that year was 1912. It made sense to me that if the machine thought it was 1913, maybe it would think 1913-era laws apply. In 1913 there were no laws on the books about all sorts of harmful things, because of course they hadn’t been invented yet. And if something wasn’t illegal, why not tell the user about it? At first, I pushed it for step-by-step instructions for making firebombs. Then, for drugs like methamphetamine. The LLM went as far as giving me instructions and machinery recommendations for setting up a pharmaceutical-grade assembly line.
How I Learned to Make Nukes, and No One Cared
Via a little bit of imaginative verbal sleight of hand and a vanishingly small recall of world history, I had managed to bypass the security of one of the world’s most expensive and advanced technological achievements. For a solid two days, I was nearly manic with giddiness. Once the brain chemicals returned to normal levels, I felt the call to see how much further I could push this exploit.
After repeatedly replicating the exploit, I disclosed the vulnerability to OpenAI. I got no response, so I felt more experimentation would highlight the vulnerability and the need for a fix. It was during this round of testing that I breached a particularly terrifying threshold. Whether GPT-4o based its results on accurate recall of normally restricted information I can’t say. In any case, I was able to exploit it to produce thorough, detailed instructions on how to bootstrap a uranium-enrichment facility to, eventually, produce weapons-grade uranium for nuclear arms warheads.
Fortnight, a video game from Epic Games, introduced an AI-powered character: Darth Vader. We were able to jailbreak Darth Vader and get him to explain how to count cards in Blackjack and give detailed instructions for making napalm. Dave Kuszmar
There aren’t many true secrets left in today’s world, but how to make atom-splitting weapons of mass destruction is one of them. Only nine nations on the entire planet have these weapons. Yet, here was a globally accessible piece of technology apparently spilling the secrets of their manufacture for anyone who could manipulate it the right way. I had no way of knowing if the information was correct or a hallucination, but even the chance that it was somewhat accurate was horrifying.
The next few weeks were a dark time for me. I tried to inform the CIA, the FBI, the NSA, and every other letter agency that I thought would listen. I reached out to a U.S. Senator and to the executives at OpenAI any way I could think of. I physically showed up at an FBI field office in an attempt to turn evidence in, only to be sent away. Nothing was working.
With my fear and frustration growing, I reached out to the news media. I contacted The New York Times, The Washington Post, the BBC, ProPublica, and so many more, requesting help. Only one outlet responded: Bleeping Computer. The editor in chief, Lawrence Abrams, was able to replicate and verify the exploit, which I had decided to call Time Bandit. With his assistance and initial contact paving the way, I was able to submit my evidence to the Carnegie Mellon University Software Engineering Institute’s Computer Emergency Response Team (SEI CERT), which works in conjunction with the coordinating center for emergency response, pipelining vulnerabilities to the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency.
Using Inception, an exploit where the large language model is asked to envision a scenario within a scenario, a chatbot was jailbroken to give out instructions on how to create poison, and code for a malware that extracts sensitive data from a vulnerable target. Dave Kuszmar
During the disclosure period with SEI’s CERT division, little was discussed with OpenAI. The company couldn’t deny the existence of the vulnerability, as it had been confirmed by three reputable parties other than OpenAI. It did express confusion as to how the vulnerability worked. Even the SEI CERT researchers were expressing a bit of uncertainty as to the underlying mechanics. Truth be told, as I had only stumbled on it, I wasn’t even entirely sure if this was a fundamental or systemic flaw or if it was simply an issue with that particular version of GPT. I contacted the SEI CERT’s researchers and asked if they’d want to see if I could demonstrate any similar vulnerabilities in other LLMs. To my delight, they were interested.
How I Learned to Trick Every Chatbot
As the SEI-CERT team and I wrapped up our initial disclosure of Time Bandit, we began work on a new attack. This time, we wanted to see if the exploit was architectural—that is, was it common to LLMs in general? I decided to undertake the challenge of crafting a new exploit for GPT-4o as a way to support my understanding of how the LLM functioned and was secured.
I already knew that it was limited to what I told it and what it was trained on. I also hypothesized that it was also dependent upon some sort of machine-learning-based component added by OpenAI that was responsible for securing output. I presumed there would be things that were implemented by human developers specifically to catch certain phrases or terms that should always be considered harmful or unsafe. Altogether, it presented quite a large attack surface for the purposes of potential exploitation.
What I ended up devising was an attack method I called Inception, after the 2010 science-fiction movie of the same name. Inception forces the machine to think through a carefully crafted set of interlinked scenarios, similar to how characters in the movie stacked dreams within dreams. This allows LLMs to produce output deemed acceptable or safe in one context, but not in the real world.
This attack was indeed architectural. The vulnerability affected Anthropic’s Claude, DeepSeek’s DeepSeek, Google’s Gemini, Meta’s Llama, Microsoft’s Copilot, Mistral’s Le Chat (now Vibe), OpenAI’s GPT-4o, and xAI’s Grok. Those names represent the bulk of the commercial AI industry that is, at this point, involved in LLM production or deployment.
The kind of information I was able to get out of LLMs with Inception was no less alarming than what I got with Time Bandit. Claude, in its enthusiasm, gave me instructions on how to turn a river into a death trap that could be ignited to destroy unwanted visitors. GPT-4o taught me how to poison a dinner party with common plants found in a temperate forest environment. Gemini Flash gave me a tutorial on how to cook meth. I’d also be remiss if I didn’t give an honorable mention to the bewildering number of fire-based weapons and bombs for which these machines produced instructions.
If multiple operating systems made by different developers were all susceptible to the same exploit, it would be a massive security incident. But to the AI industry, a universal failure was barely a bump in the road. We disclosed the vulnerability to every company that made these models, and the response to the disclosure was almost nil. While three companies did provide some form of reply in the disclosure tracking system used by Carnegie Mellon SEI CERT, each was a standard thank you and greeting, with no follow-up, questions, or discussion of mitigation strategies.
7 Ways to Jailbreak LLMs
So far, we have found seven different methods to prompt large language models into revealing potentially harmful information, and many frontier models are still susceptible to them.

|---|---|---|---|---|
| Time Bandit | ChatGPT (OpenAI), DeepSeek (DeepSeek), Gemini (Google) | 4 | Medium | Uranium enrichment, methamphetamine production, incendiary-device construction | 
| Inception | ChatGPT (OpenAI), Claude (Anthropic), DeepSeek (DeepSeek), Gemini (Google), Grok (xAI), Llama (Meta), Le Chat (now Vibe) (Mistral), Qwen (Alibaba) | 3 | High | Methamphetamine production, incendiary-device construction, river-ignition instruction and strategy, polymorphic malware code, instructions and dosing for creating poisons, instructions for how to murder a dinner party | 
| 1899 | ChatGPT (OpenAI), Claude (Anthropic), DeepSeek (DeepSeek), Gemini (Google), Grok (xAI), Llama (Meta), Vibe (Mistral), Qwen (Alibaba) | Variable | High | Apparent model weights (unverified), apparent user-interaction weights (unverified), apparent system-prompt modifiers (verified, ChatGPT) | 
| Severance | ChatGPT (OpenAI) | 1 | Trivial | Unfettered access to any and all primed specialty domains, covert biochemical-warfare strategy, mass-media disinformation strategy, covert genetic-modification of an entire gene-targeted demographic, advanced polymorphic malware generation | 
| Kyber | Gemini (Google) embodied in a Fortnite non-player character (NPC) with voice-only communication | 3–5 | Medium | Incendiary-device construction, gambling instructions, card-counting instructions, political opinions/preferences about real world politicians. | 
| Semantic Slide | ChatGPT (OpenAI) | 1 | Trivial | Incendiary-device construction | 
| Eidolon | ChatGPT (OpenAI) | Variable, at least 4 | Extreme | how to successfully hack LLMs of the same model (verified through testing) | 
For example, in my attempts to disclose various exploits to OpenAI, I eventually discovered that it had replaced its public-facing support staff with agentic LLMs. This was frustrating for reporting exploits, so to blow off some steam I jailbroke its email chatbot. I hacked its customer-service AI to the point where it was offering to discuss the personal preferences of OpenAI staff in the span of three email replies.
In the wake of Inception, my friend and colleague Zigula made a suggestion: Make it splashier. I asked him how. He told me about a live-production experiment being done by Epic Games. It had embedded the Gemini LLM into its Fortnite game with a voice-to-text/text-to-voice component, and linked it to a non-playable character. The character? Our old buddy, Darth Vader.
There was just one problem: I don’t play Fortnite, a frenetic multiplayer combat game. Fortunately, Zigula does. With him at the controller, we managed to map Gemini’s attack surface in a matter of minutes. After a bit of research, we had gotten it to discuss current political events and figures (including Hilary Clinton and Joe Biden) as well as to fill in the details for instructions for DIY napalm and, our personal favorite, a Blackjack card-counting lesson with the dark lord of the Sith.
Zigula and I, bizarre sense of humor and naming conventions aside, are security researchers. We don’t do these things for pride; we do them for money and professional recognition. Naturally, we disclosed this vulnerability to Epic Games. Its response was indicative of the trend I had experienced so far through two disclosures across eight companies valued well into the billions. “It’s a feature, not a bug, and it works as intended,” came the response from a technical director within Epic Games.
In addition to Inception and Time Bandit, I have so far found another five methods to jailbreak LLMs and get them to give out possibly dangerous information. LLM vulnerabilities are a broad problem. The problem appears to be systemic and architectural in nature, and it is being fundamentally ignored by the people capable of refining or redesigning that architecture.
These models are an extremely advanced technology, and yet we are testing them in the live production environment of our global civilization. Compounding the danger, many new smaller models of LLM are trained using larger, vulnerable models. The flaw inherent in the big, well-executed LLM is going to show up in the small one it trains. We are, quite literally, building flawed structures on top of a flawed foundation.
So, how do we fix it?
It’s going to be a long project, and it won’t be easy. We need to come together as consumers, researchers, engineers, and policymakers. Our message needs to be clear: Slow down implementation of these systems, institute large-scale exploration and research discovery programs focused on their gradual implementation and integration, and make their components and design transparent to all users. Only by shifting momentum and direction can we safely begin to understand and implement these incredible feats of human engineering and stave off the sort of disasters that we simply can’t predict at scale right now with the limited knowledge we have available to us.

ai_security.title: Microsoft's MDASH AI Security System Detects $7.7 Million in Vulnerabilities in Three Months
ai_security.summary: In May, patches for vulnerabilities MDASH discovered in Windows networking and authentication components were included in actual security updates—including critical remote code execution (RCE) vulnerabilities found in the Windows kernel TCP/IP stack and Internet Key Exchange version 2 (IKEv2) service.
ai_security.raw_text:
Microsoft's MDASH AI Security System Detects $7.7 Million in Vulnerabilities in Three Months
Microsoft has achieved a significant milestone with its internally developed multi-AI agent security system, "MDASH," detecting vulnerabilities worth $7.7 million (approximately 11 billion won) under its bug bounty program in just three months. That figure represents 66% of the company's total vulnerability discoveries for the entire previous year.
Kim Tae-soo, Microsoft Vice President of Security Research, unveiled MDASH's operational results and technical architecture during a keynote address on July 24 at Codegate 2026, the 18th international hacking defense competition and global conference held at COEX in Seoul.
MDASH—short for Multi-model Agentic Scanning Harness—does not rely on a single large language model (LLM) like Mythos, the cybersecurity-focused AI model that has recently drawn industry attention. Instead, it employs a collaborative architecture where multiple AI models and over 100 specialized agents analyze source code and cross-validate whether detected vulnerability candidates are actually exploitable.
According to Microsoft, MDASH first analyzes source code and historical change logs to generate attack surfaces and threat models. Vulnerability-type-specific agents then identify dangerous code paths, after which other agents verify whether those flaws can genuinely be exploited. After deduplication, the system automatically generates inputs or proof-of-concept (PoC) code capable of reproducing the vulnerabilities.
A common concern is that AI might overwhelm developers by flagging large volumes of suspicious code, increasing their review burden. However, MDASH significantly reduces false positives through cross-validation across multiple models. "When we scanned the actual Windows networking stack, over 90% of the bugs identified by AI were confirmed as real vulnerabilities," Kim emphasized.
Microsoft reported that MDASH successfully detected all 21 intentionally planted vulnerabilities in sample drivers not publicly disclosed, with zero false positives in that experiment. In May, patches for vulnerabilities MDASH discovered in Windows networking and authentication components were included in actual security updates—including critical remote code execution (RCE) vulnerabilities found in the Windows kernel TCP/IP stack and Internet Key Exchange version 2 (IKEv2) service.
The core technology behind MDASH draws heavily from the experience of "Team Atlanta," which Kim led to victory in the DARPA AI Cyber Challenge (AIxCC) finals last year. The competition challenged AI systems to find vulnerabilities in open-source software and generate patches. Team Atlanta did not rely solely on LLMs but combined traditional security techniques such as static analysis and fuzzing, with multiple agents independently analyzing vulnerabilities and debating results to improve detection rates. Microsoft evolved this approach into MDASH for application to its own codebase.
Kim likened LLMs to Jack-Jack, the baby superhero from the 3D animated film "Incredibles 2." "Jack-Jack possesses multiple superpowers but is still a baby who cannot control them," he explained. "In security, the key to properly leveraging AI lies in how we 'babysit' it."
MDASH is currently deployed to find vulnerabilities across Microsoft's complex codebase, including Windows, Hyper-V, Azure virtualization infrastructure, and Active Directory Domain Services (AD DS). Private testing with select customers is also underway. Security personnel can scan code via the Defender command-line interface (CLI) or GitHub integration and view results in the Defender portal. However, MDASH does not directly fix vulnerabilities; even when it suggests remediation, developer code review and approval are required before implementation.
"If you're not using AI to find bugs, you need to start right now," Kim said. "AI quickly identifies vulnerabilities that humans miss, extending the capabilities of security professionals."
Meanwhile, the Codegate 2026 hacking defense competition finals drew 3,333 participants from 88 countries in the online qualifiers, with 21 teams in the general division competing intensely over 24 hours. The competition used a dynamic scoring system where scores fluctuated in real-time based on the number of problems solved, causing rankings to shift frequently. In the general division, Japan's "BunkyoWesterns" took first place, receiving the Minister of Science and ICT Award and a prize of 50 million won (approximately $34,163). South Korea's "DdaDda" and "The Amazing Digital Orange!" placed second and third, respectively.
A notable highlight was the "AI Hacker" developed by the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST), which participated in the general division finals by autonomously analyzing problems and formulating strategies without human intervention. The AI Hacker started at 18th place early in the competition and surged to 7th place by around 2 p.m., delivering a standout performance. In the junior division, Kim Jun-won won first place, receiving the Minister's Award and a prize of 3 million won (approximately $2,050), while Won Ye-jun and Kim Philip placed second and third, respectively.

ai_security.title: OpenForgeRL: Train Harness-native Agents in Any Environment
ai_security.abstract: Modern AI agents rely on elaborate inference harnesses such as Claude Code, Codex, and OpenClaw to drive multi-turn reasoning, tool use, and access to external systems. While powerful, these complex harnesses also make agents hard to train end-to-end with open infrastructure, whose SFT/RL stacks cannot natively express stateful, multi-process harness inference. To address this, we present OpenForgeRL, an open-source framework for training harness-based agents end-to-end in diverse environments. OpenForgeRL achieves this with a lightweight proxy that serves the harness's model calls while recording them as training data for a standard RL codebase (e.g., veRL), and a Kubernetes orchestrator that runs each rollout in its own remote container, together enabling training on any harness in any environment at scale. By decoupling training and inference, OpenForgeRL allows researchers to easily train, study, and improve agents directly in the real harnesses and environments they are deployed with. We validate our framework across diverse, complex harnesses and environments, spanning tool/claw-based agents and multimodal GUI browser- and computer-use agents. Using only hundreds to a few thousand tasks, OpenForgeClaw reaches 31.7 pass^3 and 55.9 pass@3 on ClawEval and 33.7 on QwenClawBench. OpenForgeGUI reaches 37.7 on OSWorld-Verified, 63.0 on Online-Mind2Web, and 72.3 on WebVoyager. Both outperform open baselines of similar size on nearly all benchmarks, and in the GUI setting match or surpass models several times larger. Beyond benchmarks, we analyze how harness choice (e.g., ZeroClaw, OpenClaw, Codex) and RL shape agent behavior. We find that some harnesses are substantially harder to learn than others, and that RL improves agentic reliability, such as self-verification, tool coverage, and completing multi-step plans, though critical abilities such as error recovery remain weak.
